item.title: JavaScript: How to Get URL Query Parameters
item.description:
“JavaScript: How to Get URL Query Parameters”

How can we reliably extract these values using JavaScript?

Here are several effective methods, each with its own advantages, to get URL query parameters in JavaScript.

Solution 1: Vanilla JavaScript with URLSearchParams

The modern and recommended approach utilizes the URLSearchParams API. It provides a clean and straightforward way to work with query strings.

// Example URL: http://example.com?sent=yes
let searchParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);

// Check if a parameter exists
console.log(searchParams.has('sent')); // Output: true

// Get the value of a parameter
let paramValue = searchParams.get('sent');
console.log(paramValue); // Output: "yes"

// Handle multiple values for the same parameter (e.g., ?id=1&id=2)
let multipleIds = searchParams.getAll('id');
console.log(multipleIds); // Output: ["1", "2"]

This method is widely supported across modern browsers and is generally the most robust option. For a deeper dive into URLSearchParams, refer to the MDN Web Docs .

item.title: jQuery .on() vs .click() Event Handling: Which is Better?
item.description:
“jQuery .on() vs .click() Event Handling: Which is Better?”

When working with JavaScript and jQuery, managing user interactions through event handling is crucial. Two common methods for attaching click events are .click() and .on(). While they might seem similar, understanding their distinctions is key to writing efficient and robust code, especially when dealing with dynamically added content.

The primary difference lies in their application, particularly concerning event delegation.

Understanding Event Delegation with .on()

Event delegation is a technique where you attach a single event listener to a parent element, and then use event bubbling to catch events from its child elements. This is particularly useful when you have elements that are added to the DOM after the initial page load, such as through AJAX requests or dynamic content generation.

item.title: jQuery SVG Element Insertion Issues: Solutions & Workarounds
item.description:
“jQuery SVG Element Insertion Issues: Solutions & Workarounds”

It appears you’re encountering a common challenge where elements appended to an SVG container using jQuery aren’t rendering on the screen, even though they might appear in the DOM inspector. This behavior stems from how browsers handle namespaces, particularly with SVG content, and jQuery’s limitations in directly managing these namespaces for SVG creation.

When you pass a markup string to jQuery’s append or html methods, it attempts to parse it as standard HTML using innerHTML. However, innerHTML is designed for HTML elements and struggles with SVG or other non-HTML XML namespaces. It lacks the context to understand that an element like <circle> belongs to the SVG namespace, leading to rendering failures.
